text.p: Gold firmed slightly at the end of the week but base metals opted not to extend gains sustained earlier. Wheat prices were mostly higher but oil eased, leaving the Commodities Research Bureau Index 0.24 points up at 241.95.
Both copper and aluminium found overhead resistance levels difficult to overcome, despite some positive inventory data, while other metals eased from initial highs to end mixed.

Copper stalled at $2,270 soon after an unexpected LME warehouse stock fall of 3,425 tonnes, and prices spent most of the session fluctuating between $2,250 and $2,260. Overhead, there is resistance around $2,280 and then $2,313, while the support is expected from $2,250 down to $2,200.

Traders expect further short-term gains, based on tight nearby spreads around Jan/Feb dates, with European physical tightness also supportive. Last three months business was at $2,255 a tonne, down $15 from Thursday.

Aluminium lost ground in line with copper's trend, but should be helped by constructive producer stock data as reported by the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) for November. Producer stocks fell 33,000 tonnes to 1.653 million tonnes, the lowest since November 1992, while fabricated inventories of 1.437 million tonnes is the lowest for over 15 years. Prices again met some producer selling above $1,600 today, and eased back to close at $1,596, down $14.
Lead pushed higher, helped by expectations cold weather in Europe will impact on replacement battery demand, and last business was at $698, up $6.

However, zinc faltered at $1,070 resistance, despite a solid 3,700-tonne inventory fall, and the market ended at $1,064, up just $1. Nickel was erratic, with gains prompted by a 678-tonne stock fall lacking followthrough, although the market was well supported on dips. Last trade was just $10 lower at $7,200.

New York precious metals futures ended higher on Friday for the second day in a row, after gold, silver and platinum greeted the new year with sharp falls earlier this week. "But the outlook for gold and silver is ultimately still bearish, with gold likely to fall further longer term to around $340 an ounce and silver may see $4.40 an ounce," Smith Barney Washington DC-based analyst Phil Tiger said. COMEX February gold closed up $1.40 an ounce at $360.20, after rallying to $360.60, testing Tuesday's intraday high. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $358.80/30, compared to the London Friday afternoon fix at $358.25, and the New York close Thursday at $357.80/359.20.

CBOT wheat futures closed mostly higher on bullish input from USDA's estimate for 1997 U.S. winter wheat acreage. USDA said U.S. farmers last fall seeded 48.222 million acres of winter wheat, well below an average of analysts' estimates for 51.4 million acres. Wheat closed 10 cents per bushel higher to 2-1/4 lower, with March down 2-1/4 at $3.87. July was up 8-1/2 cents at $3.54-1/4.

NYMEX oil prices ended lower Friday as refined products sagged under increasing gasoline supplies and lower cash prices, sending crude lower. "Gasoline has a cross to bear in the New York Harbor with a large amount of imports coming this way and distillate prices were off slightly in the (U.S.) Gulf," said Smith Barney analyst John Saucer. February gasoline ended off 0.12 cent a gallon at 70.36 cents. February heating oil ended off 0.90 cent at 72.15 cents a gallon while February crude settled 28 cents a barrel lower at $26.09.

CSCE world sugar prices fell for the fifth straight day, ending just a notch above key chart support levels, dealers said. In what was mainly a continuation of yesterday's steep decline, speculators sold into the market throughout the session. The selling pressure intensified by the day's end, though scale-down trade buying offered support at the lows into the close. Nearby March futures fell 0.08 cent a lb, to 10.64, having traded from 10.63 to 10.77.
